scope: Focused closure audit of Britain/Celtic-fringe and southern-African candidates. No record is promoted unless population, saturation, local-food and boundary gates are all independently met.

records.label: Wales around 1290-1300: bounded population but no saturation label
records.interval_semantics: Campbell and Barry provide a 0.25-0.33 million reconstruction; Schofield reports no more than 0.30 million. The low/high envelope records the published competing bounds, not a fitted capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: Schofield (Wales and the Great Famine, 2023, pp. 8-10) reports Wales at only 14.49 people/km2 versus England's 33/km2, with most deanery units below English county densities; this is evidence against a national Malthusian ceiling.
The same review (pp. 8-10) records a local exception at Senghennydd in Glamorgan, where partible inheritance created intense competition for arable holdings by the early fourteenth century.
Schofield (pp. 10-12) describes an oat-, cattle- and pasture-based mixed economy, including transhumance and extensive upland use, but no quantitative resource-saturation calculation.
shock_flags: 1315-22 famine overlaps the later part of the period
records.food_regime: oats, cattle, sheep, pasture/transhumance, gardens and limited cereals
records.boundary_description: Former principality/Wales island of the EU5 Wales area; the historical Taxatio/deanery units are not identical to EU5 internal locations, but the national island boundary is exact.
records.notes: Rejected for training: the population interval is defensible and the EU5 national boundary is exact, but no independent saturation fraction exists; national pressure is explicitly low/heterogeneous, and no calorie-based local-food share is published. Retain as a low-pressure regional diagnostic and as a test against false continental balancing.

records.label: Scotland around 1290: population reconstruction without Malthusian pressure evidence
records.interval_semantics: Campbell's demographic synthesis brackets Scotland at about 0.64-0.94 million and treats 0.75 million as a reasonable point; these are population reconstructions, not resource-capacity labels.
pressure_evidence: Campbell (2008, Benchmarking medieval economic development, PDF pp. 935-936) estimates 0.64-0.94 million and notes that land scarcity was not a significant economic problem except locally.

The same discussion states that Scotland had about one-sixth of England's agrarian resources and that the lowland/upland split is decisive; this is a resource-endowment comparison, not evidence of national saturation.

The 1290 Scottish economy was overwhelmingly agrarian but had overseas wool/hide trade; the trade share and imported manufactured goods prevent a local-food fraction from being inferred from population alone.
shock_flags: Wars of Independence begin in the interval
records.food_regime: lowland oats/barley, pastoral livestock, fisheries, and upland mixed farming
records.boundary_description: Modern Scotland split into EU5 Scottish Highlands and Scottish Lowlands areas; the national selector exactly covers both, but the historical source does not resolve their internal boundaries.
records.notes: Rejected for training: exact national mapping and a population interval are available, but the principal source explicitly denies national land-scarcity pressure and gives no saturation or local-food calorie interval.

records.label: Ireland around 1290-1300: broad population range and unresolved resource equilibrium
records.interval_semantics: Campbell (2008, pp. 936-937) summarizes a 0.7-1.4 million range and considers the upper end plausible; it is a broad demographic reconstruction with substantial uncertainty, not an equilibrium capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: Campbell (pp. 936-937 and 940) describes substantial twelfth/thirteenth-century settlement advance but concludes that Ireland's post-1290 difficulties were not caused by resource scarcity; fighting, livestock disease, weather and terms of trade dominated.
The source estimates roughly 40 people per square mile for the island and emphasizes cattle wealth, low monetization and political fragmentation; no independent resource-pressure threshold is given.

The Irish economy exported wool/hides and remained dependent on external markets for parts of its commercial economy, so population cannot be treated as a locally supported food-equilibrium observation.
shock_flags: Lordship boundary differs from the island
records.food_regime: cattle and pastoral products, oats/barley, mixed local farming, fisheries and regional trade
records.boundary_description: Whole Ireland island represented by the four EU5 Ireland areas (Connaught, Munster, Ulster, Leinster); Campbell's Lordship-of-Ireland subset is not substituted for the island.
records.notes: Rejected for training: even the best available population range has no saturation or local-food fraction, and the source's causal conclusion is that resource scarcity was not the dominant post-1290 constraint.

records.label: Mapungubwe cultural landscape at its thirteenth-century height
records.interval_semantics: SANParks provides an archaeological lower bound of at least 9,000 people; no upper bound or ecological carrying capacity is published for the full landscape.
pressure_evidence: SANParks' site history states that the Mapungubwe landscape sustained at least 9,000 people between AD 1220 and 1300.
The same source identifies local sorghum, millet, beans and cowpeas, plus cattle/sheep/goats, wild game and Limpopo fish; this is strong qualitative local-food evidence but no calorie share.

UNESCO describes the heyday landscape as extending over approximately 30,000 km2 across the Limpopo and Shashe rivers and notes a post-1300 decline in population density, but supplies no saturation fraction.
records.food_regime: sorghum, millet, beans, cowpeas, livestock, river fish, game and gathered foods
records.boundary_description: Mapungubwe archaeological landscape across the Limpopo/Shashe region; the EU5 `mapungubwe` location is a broad proxy and not the 30,000 km2 archaeological boundary.
records.notes: Retain only as a one-sided lower-bound validation case. It cannot train scale because the full landscape is not mapped to EU5, no carrying-capacity upper bound exists, and the site's trade role prevents a local-food fraction from being inferred.

records.label: Great Zimbabwe site and catchment: ecological population model without a capacity fraction
records.interval_semantics: Chirikure et al. (PLOS ONE 2017, abstract and Tables 2-3) estimate 2,756-4,823 under a simultaneous-hut model and conclude the site population was unlikely to exceed 10,000 over the occupational sequence. These are site-population bounds, not a local Malthusian capacity interval.
pressure_evidence: Chirikure et al. (2017, PLOS ONE abstract; pp. 264-280) combine hut counts, occupation phases, ethnographic household sizes and demographic consistency checks to reject the older 18,000-20,000 estimate.

Their ecological checks (pp. 299-306, 318-324) find land and pasture readily available, low population pressure, rotating fields and transhumance; this is evidence against saturation, not independent saturation at the observed population.
The site participated in long-distance Indian Ocean trade (pp. 183-186), so the urban site cannot label intrinsic surrounding land capacity without a catchment boundary and import accounting.
shock_flags: Surrounding catchment is much larger than the EU5 site proxy
Ecological model is an upper-consistency check, not a census
records.food_regime: local sorghum/millet agriculture, livestock, pasture/transhumance, game and trade-mediated surplus
records.boundary_description: Great Zimbabwe archaeological site (720 ha) and its wider resource catchment; EU5 contains only a broad `great_zimbabwe` location in Save, not a 720 ha archaeological polygon.
records.notes: Rejected for training: the study is valuable evidence against inflated city labels and for a low-pressure negative control, but it has no cited local-calorie share, no saturation fraction and no EU5 archaeological catchment boundary.
